articles.title: Roadworks on A664 Manchester Road Scheduled from 7 September 2026
articles.excerpt: Roadworks on A664 Manchester Road in Rochdale will begin on 7 September 2026, affecting traffic flow and access to Bolton Road.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has announced that roadworks on A664 Manchester Road will commence on Monday, 7 September 2026, and are expected to last until Friday, 11 September 2026. The works will take place nightly from 8pm to 5am, during which time vehicles will be temporarily prohibited from turning left from A664 Manchester Road onto Bolton Road.

The roadworks are part of ongoing improvements in the area and will affect traffic flow significantly. Drivers are advised to use alternative routes, including A58 Manchester Road northbound, Edinburgh Road southbound, and U-turns at the roundabout, to navigate around the restrictions.

In addition to the A664 Manchester Road works, another set of roadworks is scheduled to begin on Constantine Road from 9 October 2026. This will involve a complete closure of the road for its entire length from 10pm on 9 October until 5am on 10 October, with no alternative route available for vehicles, although access will be maintained for emergency and delivery vehicles.

Local residents and commuters are encouraged to plan their journeys accordingly and stay updated on the progress of the roadworks through the Rochdale Borough Council website, where a map of ongoing works across Greater Manchester can also be viewed.

articles.title: Rochdale Borough Council Set to Acquire Warwick Mill for Regeneration
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Borough Council is preparing to take ownership of Warwick Mill, with a major regeneration announcement for Middleton town centre expected on 7 September.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council is understood to be preparing to take ownership of Warwick Mill, a significant step in the ongoing regeneration efforts for Middleton town centre. While the acquisition has not yet been formally confirmed, details are anticipated to be revealed at the 'Our Town, Our Future' event scheduled for Monday, 7 September.

The event will take place at Middleton Arena and is expected to include a major announcement regarding the regeneration of the town centre, alongside the results of a consultation involving nearly 2,500 residents and businesses. This consultation aims to gather local input on future developments and improvements.

In addition to the Warwick Mill announcement, the event will also highlight the first year of the Middleton Co-operative Mayoral Development Corporation. Key figures, including Rose Marley and Steve Coogan, co-chairs of the development corporation, will be in attendance, along with Rochdale Borough Council leader Councillor Neil Emmott and councillors June West and Dylan Williams.

The council was approached for comment regarding the acquisition but did not respond by the time of publication. Local residents and businesses are encouraged to attend the event to learn more about the future of Middleton town centre and the role Warwick Mill will play in its revitalisation.

articles.title: Rochdale Sees Rise in Avoidable Deaths Linked to Alcohol, Drugs and Smoking
articles.excerpt: A recent report reveals a rise in avoidable deaths in Rochdale, primarily due to alcohol and drug use. Health officials outline strategies to address these issues, including new treatment pathways and community initiatives.
articles.content_html:
A report by Rochdale health officials has revealed a concerning rise in avoidable deaths within the borough, primarily linked to alcohol and drug use. The findings indicate that while the number of people drinking has not increased, the harm caused by alcohol consumption is escalating, particularly following the Covid-19 pandemic in 2020.

According to the National Drug Treatment Monitoring System (NDTMS), there are approximately 2,905 individuals in Rochdale who are dependent on alcohol. The report highlights that alcohol-related death rates in the area are significantly higher than the national average. Additionally, around 1,831 residents are estimated to use opiates and crack cocaine, further contributing to the rising mortality rates.

In response to these alarming statistics, the local authority has outlined several measures aimed at reducing alcohol and drug consumption. These include the development of a refreshed drug and alcohol policy for schools, increased outreach and follow-up services for vulnerable groups, and the establishment of a new treatment pathway specifically for crack cocaine users. Furthermore, the council plans to collaborate with Trading Standards to combat underage sales of addictive substances.

The report emphasises the need for a collective approach to tackle addiction, which is described as a chronic condition influenced by various social factors. Community initiatives, including stop smoking programmes and health checks, are also being expanded to address smoking rates, which currently stand at 12.7% in Rochdale, above the national average of 10.9%. The council aims to implement these strategies by September 2026, with the hope of significantly reducing avoidable deaths in the borough.

articles.title: New £12 Million Storage World Building Planned for Old Hall Street in Middleton
articles.excerpt: Self-Storage Performance Management International Ltd has submitted plans to Rochdale Council for a new mixed-use building on Old Hall Street, designed to reflect Middleton's mill heritage and replace a facility destroyed by fire.
articles.content_html:
Self-Storage Performance Management International Ltd (SSPMI) has submitted a planning application to Rochdale Council for a new mixed-use building on Old Hall Street in Middleton. The proposed development, which is estimated to cost £12 million, aims to replace the previous Storage World facility that was destroyed by fire in June 2025.

The new building will feature a self-storage facility along with commercial units on the ground floor. Although it will occupy half the space of the former Storage World building, it will include two additional storeys to maintain the same storage capacity. The site previously housed the four-storey Albany Mill, constructed in 1884 and demolished in 1976, which was later replaced by a two-storey warehouse operated by Comfy Quilts until its relocation in 2006.

SSPMI acquired the site in 2013 and opened it as FlexiSpace in 2016, later rebranding it as Storage World. Following the fire, the company has been collaborating with Rochdale Development Agency and Middleton Mayoral Development Corporation to design a replacement that complements the ongoing regeneration efforts in the area.

The new Storage World building is intended to reflect Middleton's industrial heritage while also looking towards the future. The design aims to honour the site's historical significance while providing modern facilities for the community. The planning decision is expected to be made by Rochdale Council in the coming months.

articles.title: Why Rochdale says ‘cruckle’
articles.excerpt: A short guide to the little local verb: what ‘cruckle’ means, where it comes from and why linguists care that Rochdalians still use it.
articles.summary: A short guide to the little local verb: what ‘cruckle’ means, where it comes from and why linguists care that Rochdalians still use it.
articles.body:
Anyone from parts of Rochdale will recognise the complaint: “I cruckled my ankle.” The small verb cruckle is used locally to mean rolling or twisting one’s ankle — the awkward, often walk‑offable misstep that still makes you wince. That everyday meaning is recorded in contemporary local projects and described by linguists working on Greater Manchester speech. (It’s not a medical term — cruckle simply names the action of turning your foot over.)

Why is it so strongly linked with Rochdale? Recent perceptual‑dialect research — the kind of work that asks hundreds of local people to mark and label accents and words on maps — shows that residents routinely associate particular words with particular boroughs. In a 2024 study of Greater Manchester folk‑linguistic labels, participants’ free comments listed “cruckle/cruckled” alongside other Rochdale items, which places the word in the borough’s visible local vocabulary. That kind of folk mapping is what gives a word social life: people hear it, use it and then point to it as a marker of place. (Researchers describe the method as a modified draw‑a‑map task, and they use GIS to show where labels cluster.)

Cruckle is not a recent invention. Historical dialect material shows an older verb crookle (also spelled in various ways) with senses such as “to bend, make crooked, stoop or hobble.” Those meanings sit in the same semantic field as the modern Rochdale use: bending or twisting, and the small repetitive‑action suffix ‑le is typical of many northern English dialect verbs. In short, cruckle looks like a local survival or variant of an older dialect verb family that originally meant “to make crooked” and later narrowed to the specific action of rolling an ankle in everyday Rochdale speech.

How exclusive is the word to Rochdale? Dialect researchers are cautious: administrative borders are poor predictors of where a word will or won’t be used. Perceptual studies and regional projects show that cruckle is highly salient in Rochdale (people there report and recognise it), and national and regional reports on Manchester‑area speech list “cruckled” under Rochdale. But similar or related forms (crookle, crukle) have been recorded historically elsewhere in northern and midland dialect glossaries. That means the form’s current social visibility is especially strong in Rochdale, even if related forms exist in historical records outside the borough.

Why should readers care? Tiny local verbs like cruckle are more than quaint curios. They are living traces of regional history, contact and sound change: the shape of the word (crook → crookle → cruck­le), the suffix pattern and the local social practice of using the word are all pieces of evidence linguists use to map how language marks identity. Projects that collect local voices — from university‑led “accent van” recordings to academic perceptual mapping — treat items like cruckle as precisely the sort of everyday data that shows how place and speech stay linked.

If you’ve got family examples, old spellings or a recording of someone saying the word, local archives and dialect projects welcome them. Contributions from speakers help researchers pin down where a word is used today and how its meaning has shifted over time. For now, the answer to “Why does Rochdale say cruckle?” is straightforward: people in Rochdale do say it, it names a recognisable action (rolling your ankle), it fits an old dialect pattern (crookle → cruckle), and perceptual dialect research shows the word is part of Rochdale’s local linguistic identity — even if identical forms turn up elsewhere in older records.

articles.content_html:
BREAKING NEWS — LIVE

Live updates, newest first.

15:47, 04 September 2026

A man was arrested by student police officers in Rochdale town centre after being spotted wearing a balaclava and acting suspiciously. He is wanted in connection with multiple alleged offences.

Student police officers on patrol in Rochdale town centre arrested a man wearing a balaclava who was acting suspiciously near the central bus station on Friday, 4 September 2026. The officers, part of Greater Manchester Police (GMP), conducted a stop search and recovered a bank card believed to be stolen.

Further investigations revealed that the man was wanted in connection with multiple alleged breaches of bail conditions. He was subsequently arrested on suspicion of theft and breach of bail offences and remains in police custody while enquiries continue.

Inspector Meena Yasin, of Rochdale North neighbourhood policing, stated that this arrest highlights their proactive commitment to maintaining safety in Rochdale town centre. She emphasised that anyone acting suspiciously can expect to be engaged by police officers during their patrols.

GMP Rochdale shared that their student officers are regularly patrolling the area to deter criminal activity and positively engage with the public, contributing to community safety.

articles.title: Horse in Rochdale left critically ill after being fed harmful food by campers
articles.excerpt: A horse owner in Rochdale is seeking awareness after her horse, Frank, fell critically ill due to being fed harmful scraps by campers. The incident has raised concerns about the dangers of feeding horses human food.
articles.content_html:
A horse in Rochdale has been left in a critical condition after being fed something dangerous by campers, according to his owner, Julie Kershaw. The incident occurred when Julie, 58, discovered her 13-year-old horse, Frank, trembling and unable to walk in the field where he is kept. Julie believes that the campers fed Frank human food, which led to his distress and subsequent health issues.

Julie was alerted to Frank's condition by her daughter, who was out walking with a friend when they found the horse shaking uncontrollably and struggling to breathe. They quickly issued a Facebook appeal to locate Julie, who rushed to the scene. Upon arrival, she found Frank in a dire state, fearing he would not survive the night. Julie stated, "He was really shaking and couldn't walk," highlighting the severity of the situation.

A vet was called and arrived within 40 minutes, administering four injections to treat Frank's condition, which was diagnosed as colitis, an infection in the colon. The emergency visit resulted in a vet bill of £235, with additional costs for food bringing the total to around £300. Julie expressed her frustration, stating, "It's just so scary - people don't realise how dangerous it is to feed horses."

This incident is not isolated; Julie noted that horse owners in the area have previously found harmful items such as chicken bones and vegetables discarded in fields. She urged the public to educate themselves on what is safe to feed horses, emphasising that even common treats can become dangerous if overfed. Julie's experience serves as a reminder of the potential risks associated with feeding horses human food.

articles.title: Are there really fairies in Healey Dell?
articles.excerpt: The Fairies’ Chapel is a real, water‑carved nook of rock that has gathered centuries of stories — but folklore and documentary record tell very different tales.
articles.summary: The Fairies’ Chapel is a real, water‑carved nook of rock that has gathered centuries of stories — but folklore and documentary record tell very different tales.
articles.body:
Walk under the stone viaduct at Healey Dell and you’ll find a narrow cleft where the River Spodden thunders through a rocky throat. Local signs and the Healey Dell Heritage Centre point visitors to a spot long called the Fairies’ Chapel — an evocative name that has attracted guidebooks, children’s trails and Victorian collectors of legend alike. The site is part of Healey Dell Nature Reserve, managed and promoted by Rochdale Borough Council as a place of industrial archaeology, woodland and waterfalls. ([rochdale.gov.uk](https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/directory-record/737/healey-dell-nature-reserve-and-tea-rooms-rochdale))

What is indisputable: the place and its industrial history are real. The high stone viaduct that dominates the valley is a Grade II‑listed Victorian structure on the National Heritage List for England, and the valley contains the remains of mills, lodges and a former railway line now used as a trail. These are documented, protected features and form the historic backdrop that helped foreground the rock seat and grotto known as the Fairies’ Chapel. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1317784))

What created the ‘chapel’ is ordinary geology and the work of water. Guides and local interpretation explain that the Thrutch — a narrow gorge — contains a small natural excavation scored by the attrition of the river; older accounts and the Healey Dell visitor material say a great flood in early July 1838 altered or destroyed some of the rock formations formerly seen there. In short: the chapel‑like shapes are the result of erosion and historic landscape change, not built masonry. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/history/Fairies-Chapel-final.pdf))

And the fairies? That is the realm of story. The best‑known accounts of the Fairies’ Chapel come from 19th‑century collectors such as John Roby, whose Traditions of Lancashire (first published in 1829 and reprinted in later nineteenth‑century editions) recorded a long narrative about a miller, a Lady Eleanor, a fortune‑teller called Mother Bagden, and encounters with fairy royalty in the Thrutch. Roby’s work, and later local retellings and guidebook extracts, mixed oral tradition, local gossip and romantic reconstruction — material to be enjoyed as folklore, not read as factual history. ([upload.wikimedia.org](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c1/Lancashire_legends_%28IA_lancashirelegend00roby%29.pdf))

Versions of the tale vary. In some tellings a Fairy King condemns witches to a rocky chapel; in others a prophecy or an enchanted hare leads a boastful miller into the fairy grotto. These stories have been printed and reworked for more than a century, and they fed Victorian visitors’ appetite for “haunted” beauty spots. The modern Healey Dell Heritage Centre preserves and retells many of these legends, and the valley’s trails now include family‑friendly interpretation such as a fairy grotto for children. Those activities keep the stories alive, but do not serve as evidence that supernatural beings live there. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/history/Fairies-Chapel-final.pdf))

So: are there really fairies in Healey Dell? If you mean literal, sentient fairies as found in the stories — no contemporary, verifiable evidence supports that claim. If you mean “are there stories, traditions and a long local appetite for the uncanny” — absolutely. The Fairies’ Chapel is a genuine landscape feature with a documented industrial and geological history; it is also a cultural site where folklore collected since the early 19th century continues to be told and enjoyed. ([rochdale.gov.uk](https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/directory-record/737/healey-dell-nature-reserve-and-tea-rooms-rochdale))

For visitors: treat the site as a meeting of nature, history and imagination. Respect the reserve’s paths and signage, enjoy the viaduct and waterfalls documented by Historic England and the borough, and bring a good torch if you try the narrow paths near the Thrutch. Above all, enjoy the stories as stories — valuable for what they tell us about local memory and the way places gather meaning over time. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1317784))

The high stone viaduct that dominates the valley is a Grade II‑listed Victorian structure on the National Heritage List for England, and the valley contains the remains of mills, lodges and a former railway line now used as a trail. These are documented, protected features and form the historic backdrop that helped foreground the rock seat and grotto known as the Fairies’ Chapel. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1317784))

What created the ‘chapel’ is ordinary geology and the work of water. Guides and local interpretation explain that the Thrutch — a narrow gorge — contains a small natural excavation scored by the attrition of the river; older accounts and the Healey Dell visitor material say a great flood in early July 1838 altered or destroyed some of the rock formations formerly seen there. In short: the chapel‑like shapes are the result of erosion and historic landscape change, not built masonry. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/history/Fairies-Chapel-final.pdf))

And the fairies? That is the realm of story. The best‑known accounts of the Fairies’ Chapel come from 19th‑century collectors such as John Roby, whose Traditions of Lancashire (first published in 1829 and reprinted in later nineteenth‑century editions) recorded a long narrative about a miller, a Lady Eleanor, a fortune‑teller called Mother Bagden, and encounters with fairy royalty in the Thrutch. Roby’s work, and later local retellings and guidebook extracts, mixed oral tradition, local gossip and romantic reconstruction — material to be enjoyed as folklore, not read as factual history. ([upload.wikimedia.org](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c1/Lancashire_legends_%28IA_lancashirelegend00roby%29.pdf))

Versions of the tale vary. In some tellings a Fairy King condemns witches to a rocky chapel; in others a prophecy or an enchanted hare leads a boastful miller into the fairy grotto. These stories have been printed and reworked for more than a century, and they fed Victorian visitors’ appetite for “haunted” beauty spots. The modern Healey Dell Heritage Centre preserves and retells many of these legends, and the valley’s trails now include family‑friendly interpretation such as a fairy grotto for children. Those activities keep the stories alive, but do not serve as evidence that supernatural beings live there. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/history/Fairies-Chapel-final.pdf))

So: are there really fairies in Healey Dell? If you mean literal, sentient fairies as found in the stories — no contemporary, verifiable evidence supports that claim. If you mean “are there stories, traditions and a long local appetite for the uncanny” — absolutely. The Fairies’ Chapel is a genuine landscape feature with a documented industrial and geological history; it is also a cultural site where folklore collected since the early 19th century continues to be told and enjoyed. ([rochdale.gov.uk](https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/directory-record/737/healey-dell-nature-reserve-and-tea-rooms-rochdale))

For visitors: treat the site as a meeting of nature, history and imagination. Respect the reserve’s paths and signage, enjoy the viaduct and waterfalls documented by Historic England and the borough, and bring a good torch if you try the narrow paths near the Thrutch. Above all, enjoy the stories as stories — valuable for what they tell us about local memory and the way places gather meaning over time. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1317784))

articles.title: Elite Hand Car Wash in Rochdale Fined for Minimum Wage Violations
articles.excerpt: Elite Hand Car Wash on Molesworth Street has been penalised for failing to pay a worker the minimum wage, as part of a government initiative naming over 600 employers.
articles.content_html:
Elite Hand Car Wash, located on Molesworth Street in Rochdale, has been penalised for failing to pay a worker the national minimum wage. The business, operated by Ms Misbah Khalil, is among 658 employers recently named by the government for similar violations.

The government initiative revealed that Elite Hand Car Wash owed £4,590.40 to one employee. This is part of a broader effort that has seen nearly £4 million returned to over 27,000 workers across the UK who were underpaid. Additionally, employers have faced penalties totalling £7 million for non-compliance with wage regulations.

The current national minimum wage is set at £12.71 per hour for workers aged 21 and over, £10.85 for those aged 18 to 20, and £8 for under-18s and apprentices. Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds emphasised the importance of treating workers fairly, stating that responsible businesses understand that looking after their employees is essential for success.

As a result of this naming and shaming initiative, Elite Hand Car Wash may face increased scrutiny from both the public and regulatory bodies. Local residents and potential customers may wish to consider this information when choosing services in the area.

articles.title: Police Seize Supercars Following Dangerous Driving Reports on M62 Near Rochdale
articles.excerpt: Greater Manchester Police seized five Lamborghinis and a Mercedes G-Wagon after reports of dangerous driving on the M66 and M62. The vehicles were stopped on September 2, 2026, and the drivers face prosecution for multiple offences.
articles.content_html:
BREAKING NEWS — LIVE

Live updates, newest first.

20:06, 03 September 2026

Greater Manchester Police seized five Lamborghinis and a Mercedes G-Wagon after reports of dangerous driving on the M66 and M62. The vehicles were stopped on September 2, 2026, and the drivers face prosecution for multiple offences.

Five Lamborghinis and a Mercedes G-Wagon were seized by Greater Manchester Police (GMP) following reports of dangerous driving on the M66 and M62 motorways on the evening of September 2, 2026.

Police received multiple reports of high-speed driving, with vehicles weaving between lanes and at times slowing to around 17mph. Officers from GMP's Transport Policing and Crime Command responded and located the convoy on the M62, stopping two Lamborghinis as they exited the motorway. Specialist tactics were employed to halt the remaining vehicles in Rochdale.

The vehicles were seized under Section 59 of the Police Reform Act 2002, and the drivers are being prosecuted for a number of driving offences. Chief Inspector Danny Kabal from GMP's Transport Policing and Crime Command stated, "We take road safety very seriously in GMP, and we will not tolerate careless, inconsiderate, anti-social or dangerous driving on our roads." He warned that those who treat roads as racetracks will face vehicle seizure and prosecution.

The police temporarily closed the road while managing the situation and thanked members of the public who reported the dangerous driving. They encouraged anyone with footage of the incident, including dashcam or CCTV recordings, to contact GMP via 101 or through their website. Road traffic footage can also be submitted through GMP's Operation Snap service.

articles.title: Rochdale Residents Urged to Check Voter Registration Ahead of May 2027 Elections
articles.excerpt: With local elections scheduled for May 2027, Rochdale Borough Council is reminding residents to verify their voter registration details to ensure they can participate in upcoming elections.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council is urging residents to check their electoral registration details to avoid losing their chance to vote in the upcoming local elections in May 2027. The council's annual canvass aims to keep the electoral register updated and to identify individuals who may risk losing their voting rights if they are not registered.

Edward McCreadie, elections manager at Rochdale Borough Council, stated that over the summer, emails were sent to residents in more than 40,000 properties, asking them to verify their details. Follow-up letters were dispatched this week, and residents are encouraged to keep an eye out for these communications. McCreadie emphasised the importance of ensuring that the information on the electoral register is accurate and up to date, saying, "To make sure you don’t lose your say at upcoming elections, simply follow the instructions sent to you."

Residents who have recently moved homes are particularly urged to check their registration status. Research from the Electoral Commission indicates that recent movers are less likely to be registered compared to those who have lived at the same address for a longer period. In Great Britain, 92% of individuals who have resided in their homes for 16 years are registered, while only 36% of those who have lived at an address for less than a year are registered.

Individuals aged 16 and above can be added to the electoral register, although they cannot vote until they reach the age of 18. Residents wishing to register can do so easily online at rochdale.gov.uk/RegisterToVote. The council's efforts aim to ensure that all eligible residents can participate in the democratic process during the forthcoming elections.
